spec.title: PROP-059 — User applications: install, launch, alternatives, storage libraries

status.comment: Clean contract adopted 2026-10-30 after the October prototype was archived (branch archive/app-overlay-prototype-2026-10). Implementation follows the APP-CLEAN campaign plan.

p.purpose: vibe is also a small cross-platform meta-distribution: a package of kind `app` describes how to install an upstream application on each supported platform, how to launch it, and which commands it puts on PATH. Several versions or providers of one application may be installed side by side; one is the global default and any shell may pick another for itself. Installed applications live in one or more storage libraries and may be moved between them.

p.principle: The implementation is as simple as the ordinary filesystem allows and no simpler. Durable state is plain files replaced atomically (write a sibling, rename over). There are no journals, checkpoints, leases, seals, witnesses, byte budgets or cold-recovery machinery. An operation interrupted half-way leaves at most an orphan directory, which `vibe storage gc` reports and removes. Missing storage is reported as unavailable, never repaired or guessed around.

p.library-first: Every capability below lives in the `vibe-app` library crate; the CLI, the PATH proxy and any future surface are thin callers (`spec://org.vibevm.world/omnichannel/flows/omnichannel/OMNICHANNEL-PROTOCOL#root`).

p.declaration: An app package has `[package] kind = "app"` and no `[project]` table. `[application]` carries `id` (the slot name, a portable token) and optional `portable` (default `true`). Installation choices live only in `[[installer_options]]`; a package with none is a valid product that `vibe install -g` refuses as not globally installable. Package-author names, never heuristics, supply displayed platform and installer names. The retired fields `installer_package`, `runtime`, `entry`, `commands`, `distribution` and the `[application_source]` table are no longer parsed. `vibe init --kind app`, in its root and its nested form, scaffolds a package that plans as written: `[application]` with `id` set to the package name, one `[[installer_options]]` (`id = "main"`) for the host platform and architecture holding one `recipe` step `build` that runs `recipes/build.sh` with `posix_sh` (`recipes/build.ps1` with `windows_powershell` on Windows), that script, and an empty `icons/` directory; no launcher is written and nothing new is asked. Every refusal of the application validators names its field as a TOML path — table names as the manifest writes them, array elements by zero-based index, the leaf field last (`installer_options[1].steps[0].sha256`) — beside its sentence, which stays as it was; `vibe check --json` reports that path as the finding's `field` (`spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/VIBEVM-SPEC#linter`).

p.installer-options: Each `[[installer_options]]` row has a stable `id`, a human `name`, `platform` id with `platform_name`, `arch` id with optional `arch_name`, optional `portable` override, optional `pre_install` / `post_install` commands, exactly one `installation` method, its `launchers` and its `public_commands`. Predefined platform ids `linux`, `windows`, `macos` and the host CPU architecture are auto-detected; other ids are selectable only explicitly. `vibe install -g` accepts `--platform`, `--arch`, `--installer`; an attended terminal asks platform, then architecture, then installer with the detected row first; an unattended ambiguity is a selection error. `vibe app installers PACKAGE --json` lists every row without installing.

p.installer-separation: `installation.type` is one of `shell`, `zip`, `tar_gz`, `exe`, `msi`, `source_build`; each is the short spelling of a one- or two-step list under `spec://org.vibevm.core/vibevm/common/PROP-065#sugar`, and an option may declare `[[steps]]` directly instead (`PROP-065#steps`). Shell: authored `install`, `force_install`, `uninstall`, `force_uninstall`, optional `update`, `app_root`, and optional `interpreter` (`posix_sh`, `windows_cmd`, `windows_powershell`; host default `posix_sh` on Linux/macOS, `windows_cmd` on Windows). Apt, Homebrew and Winget are shell commands, not kinds. Zip / tar_gz: `source` URL or package-relative path, `sha256`, optional `payload_root`. Exe / msi: `source`, `sha256`, `app_root`, `arguments`, optional `force_arguments`, `uninstall`, `force_uninstall`; they run only on Windows, EXE directly and MSI through `msiexec`. Source_build: `#source-build`. Shell, exe and msi installations are external: vibe records their `app_root` but never deletes or moves it. Zip, tar_gz and source_build installations are owned: vibe places the payload in a library directory it fully controls.

p.launch-points: Each `[[installer_options.launchers]]` row has a stable `id`, `name`, `executable` template, a required `kind` — `gui` (a window of its own), `tui` (a full-screen terminal program, opened by a graphical client through a terminal it starts) or `command` (a console program that reads arguments and prints) — declared by the package author and never inferred, optional `description`, `args`, `working_directory`, `icon` (a path or the icon set of `#menu`), `categories`, `keywords`, booleans `menu` (`#menu`), `terminal` and `default` (at most one default per option). `terminal` is derived from the kind (`true` for `tui` and `command`, `false` for `gui`); when spelled, it must agree, and `vibe check` refuses a disagreement. `[[installer_options.public_commands]]` rows map a PATH command `name` to a launcher `id` of the same option; a command name starts with a lowercase letter or digit and continues with letters, digits, `-`, `_`, `.` or `+` (`g++`, `python3.12`), never `vibe`.

p.menu: A graphical client builds a start menu and a taskbar from installed applications, and every entry in it is the package author's explicit decision. A launcher carries `menu = true` to appear there; the default is `false` for every launcher of every kind, so a package shipping a hundred executables lists none of them until the author chooses — a suite of ten utilities and one central program lists the central one, the rest stay installed and reachable through `app launchers`, `app start` and PATH. `[application] menu_group` is the human-readable name of the group the client shows this application's entries under (the way "Adobe Master Collection" is a group), independent of the package name and distinct from `description`; without it, each entry stands alone. `categories` (the freedesktop main categories: `AudioVideo`, `Audio`, `Video`, `Development`, `Education`, `Game`, `Graphics`, `Network`, `Office`, `Science`, `Settings`, `System`, `Utility`) and `keywords` may be set on `[application]` as defaults and on a launcher as its own. An icon is one package-relative path (a PNG or SVG, the short form) or an icon set: `{ svg = "…", png = { "16" = "…", "32" = "…", "48" = "…", "128" = "…", "256" = "…", "512" = "…" }, ico = "…", icns = "…", symbolic = "…", maskable = true }` — `svg` the scalable source, `png` rasters by pixel size, `ico` and `icns` ready containers, `symbolic` a monochrome variant for taskbars, trays and dark surfaces, `maskable` stating the content sits in the central 80% so a platform mask may be applied. Sizes are pixels; `@2x` and DPI scale are the client's concern, which picks the smallest raster not smaller than what it needs. A launcher's icon set overrides the application's; a client falls back from the launcher to the application to its own icon by `kind`. A package-relative icon path names a file of the package tree, which is not part of a payload: at install, vibe copies every package-relative icon file of the application and of the chosen option's launchers into `<home>/applications/icons/<key>/` keeping the relative path, for owned and external results alike; listings resolve package-relative icons there and `$app_root`-templated ones in the payload; `modify` and reinstall refresh the copies, `uninstall` removes the directory, and a storage move leaves it in place because it belongs to the home, not to the library. `vibe check` verifies that every named file exists in the package tree, that a PNG is square and matches the size it is listed under (from the header), and that a launcher with `menu = true` has at least an SVG or a PNG of 256 pixels or more; other launchers may have no icon. `describe`, `app list --json` and `app launchers --json` carry `kind`, `menu`, `menu_group`, `categories`, `keywords` and the icon set with resolved absolute paths; `vibe app launchers --all [--menu] --json` lists every ready, exposed installation of the home in one answer, `--menu` only the entries opted in; `vibe app icon PKG [--launcher ID] --size N [--prefer png|svg|symbolic|ico|icns]` prints the path of the best existing file for that size (the smallest raster not smaller than N, else the largest, else the SVG) and never rasterises. Writing system `.desktop`, `.lnk` or icon-theme files is a projection of the catalog of `#launcher-catalog`, never a second source. Reading them is `#desktop-entries`.

p.desktop-entries: The launcher model is a superset of a freedesktop desktop entry, so software that ships `.desktop` files is described once. Beyond `#menu`, a launcher may carry `generic_name` (the entry's `GenericName`, "Text editor"), `names` and `descriptions` tables keyed by language tag for localised `Name[xx]` and `Comment[xx]`, `window_class` (`StartupWMClass`, how a taskbar matches windows to the entry), `mime_types` (`MimeType`), and `[[installer_options.launchers.actions]]` rows (`[Desktop Action …]`, a jump list: `id`, `name`, `args`, optional `icon`). The `args` template accepts the placeholders `{file}`, `{files}`, `{url}` and `{urls}` for what a client opens with the launcher (`%f`, `%F`, `%u`, `%U`); `%i`, `%c` and `%k` have no counterpart and are dropped. An installer option may declare `launchers_from = ["share/applications/*.desktop"]`, globs relative to the application root: after the payload is in place, vibe reads every matching file that is an `Application` entry and not `Hidden`, and derives one launcher per file — `id` the file name without `.desktop`, `name`, `generic_name`, `description`, localised tables, `executable` and `args` from `Exec` (the first word resolved through the payload's `bin` and the PATH the launcher will have, field codes mapped as above), `working_directory` from `Path`, `kind` `tui` when `Terminal=true` else `gui`, `categories`, `keywords`, `mime_types`, `window_class`, `actions`, `menu` set to the opposite of `NoDisplay` (the author who ships the entry has decided it is shown), and the icon set from `Icon`: a path is taken as is, a theme name is collected from `share/icons/hicolor/<N>x<N>/apps/<name>.png`, `scalable/apps/<name>.svg` and `symbolic/apps/<name>-symbolic.svg` under the application root. `TryExec`, `StartupNotify`, `OnlyShowIn`, `NotShowIn`, `DBusActivatable` and `X-` keys are ignored. An authored `[[installer_options.launchers]]` row with the same `id` overrides field by field; the derived rows are recorded in the index like authored ones and `app launchers --json` marks each with `source: "authored" | "desktop-entry"`. `vibe app import-desktop FILE…` prints the same rows as manifest TOML for an author who prefers explicit text. The same key vocabulary is the natural target for Windows and macOS metadata later; nothing here is Linux-only except the derivation globs.

p.launcher-catalog: The launchers of a home are a catalog vibe serves, and a graphical client draws its own start menu, its collections in the manner of a game library, its taskbar and its recent list from that catalog instead of from the operating system's menus. `vibe app launchers --all [--menu] --json` is the catalog, `vibe-app-launchers-all/2`: the home, the `revision` below, and every launcher of every ready, exposed installation, each with a stable launcher key (`<package key>#<launcher id>`, the package key exactly as the index spells it), its package, installation and slot, `kind`, `menu`, the icon set as resolved absolute files, the localised names, `window_class`, `mime_types`, `actions`, `source`, the collections it sits in, where it is pinned, who hid it, its effective `display_name` and `display_icon` beside the package's own declaration, and the usage facts below; and per installation `state` — `hidden`, `held`, and `update_available`, which no listing answers because finding out needs a registry call (`vibe app outdated` makes it). `vibe app launchers PACKAGE --json` is one installation in the same shape, `vibe-app-launchers/2`. **User layer.** The home keeps `<home>/applications/launchers.toml` (`vibe-app-user-launchers/1`), the user's own arrangement over the catalog, edited through commands so no client writes TOML: `vibe app collection create|rename|delete|add|remove|order|list NAME …` (a collection is a named, ordered list of launcher keys with an optional icon, and a launcher may sit in several; `add` appends what the collection does not hold, `order` is the full order, and `remove` is remembered in the collection's `removed` list so a later install does not undo it), `vibe app pin|unpin KEY [--to taskbar|favorites]` (pinned lists are ordered and a repeated pin moves the key to the end), `vibe app launcher KEY --hide|--show|--name "…"|--icon PATH|--reset` (a user override of name or icon that survives update and reinstall; `--reset` returns to the package's declaration). A hidden launcher stays in the catalog marked `hidden_by: "user"`, distinct from a package that declares `menu = false`. Every edit answers the whole layer as `vibe-app-collections/1`, so a client that changed one collection sees what the change did to the rest. A key that names no launcher of the home is the refusal `launcher_missing`, a collection that does not exist `collection_missing`, and `create` of a name already taken `collection_exists` — all three before any effect. **Seeding.** `[application] menu_group` (`#menu`) seeds a collection of that name: an install, modify or update creates it when it is absent and appends the package's `menu = true` launchers that are not in it already, never reordering what the user arranged and never re-adding a key the user removed. An uninstall drops that package's keys from every collection, both pinned lists, the overrides and the usage facts, and drops a seeded collection the removal left empty that no `collection` command had touched; a collection the user edited is the user's and outlives the package. **Revision.** `<home>/applications/revision` holds one integer the home increments under its mutation lock on every change to `index.json`, `launchers.toml` or the usage facts, so a client compares one number (`vibe app launchers --revision`, `vibe-app-revision/1`) instead of the whole document. **Usage.** `<home>/applications/usage.json` keeps `starts` and `last_started` (RFC 3339) per launcher key — its own file and not part of the index, so starting a program never rewrites the inventory. The catalog carries both, so "recent" and "most used" are views, not state a client keeps. **Starting.** `vibe app start PACKAGE [--launcher ID]` and `vibe app start KEY` (a key's `#<launcher id>` selects the launch point, and `--launcher` is the other spelling of the same choice, never a second one) record the start before the program runs. With `--json` the launcher is started detached — its own process group on Unix, `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP | DETACHED_PROCESS` for a `gui` point on Windows and the console kept for `tui` and `command` — and the answer is `vibe-app-start/1`: the key, the process id, the command, the argument array, the working directory and the log `<home>/cache/app-runs/<installation>/start-<launcher>-<ts>.log` capturing its stdout and stderr, so a client drawing a start menu is not blocked by the program it launched. Without `--json` the start stays attached and passes the program's exit status through. Writing system `.desktop`, `.lnk` or icon-theme files is a projection of this catalog, never a second source. Reading them is `#desktop-entries`.

p.launcher-runtime: What a graphical client needs beside the catalog of `#launcher-catalog` to draw a taskbar and follow the home without polling. **Running.** A detached `vibe app start … --json` records `<home>/applications/running/<pid>.json` (`key`, `pid`, `started` in RFC 3339, `kind`, `command`, `log`, and the platform's own start time of the process where it gives one — field 22 of `/proc/<pid>/stat` on Linux, the creation time on Windows). `vibe app running [--json]` (`vibe-app-running/1`: `home`, `running`, `stopped`) lists the records whose process is still alive, oldest first — alive by `/proc` or `kill(pid, 0)` on Unix (a zombie is gone), by `OpenProcess` and its exit code on Windows, and a recorded start time that differs from the process's own means the id was reused and the launcher is gone — and prunes the others under the home's mutation lock, appending one `exited` event each; a lock another command holds is not waited for, the dead records simply stay until the next listing. `vibe app stop KEY|PID [--json]` takes a launcher key, a package key (every running launcher of it) or a recorded process id — never an arbitrary process — and ends each match the way `#cancellation` of PROP-065 ends a step: it asks (`SIGTERM` to the launcher's own process group on Unix; on Windows a console break for a `tui` or `command` launcher that kept the console: since `GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent` reaches only processes sharing the caller's console, `vibe app stop` detaches from its own, attaches to the launcher's (`AttachConsole`), generates `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` for the launcher's process group, then re-attaches to its parent's console; a launcher with no console to attach to is ended by the terminate branch as before), waits up to five seconds, then ends it without asking (`SIGKILL`, `TerminateProcess`); a request that cannot be delivered, such as a Windows `gui` launcher with no console to break, is not waited for. The answer lists each stopped process with `ended` — `terminated`, `killed` or `gone` (it had already exited) — beside what still runs; nothing matching is the refusal `not_running` before any effect. **Change feed.** Every call that bumps the revision appends one line to `<home>/applications/events.jsonl` under the same lock, and an exit noticed by `running`, `stop` or `watch` appends one at the current revision; the journal is rotated to `events.jsonl.1` at 256 KiB. `vibe app watch [--json]` prints one `vibe-app-events/1` line per change from the moment it starts — `event` (`installed`, `updated`, `removed`, `launchers-changed`, `collections-changed`, `started`, `exited`), the `revision` after it, `key` when there is one (a package key for an inventory change, a launcher key for `started`, `exited` and an override of one launcher), `pid` of an exited launcher, and `at` — until its standard input closes or it is interrupted. It reads the journal every 250 ms (a poll, not a file-system notification) and sweeps the running registry on the same tick, so a launcher that exits on its own is reported without anyone calling `running`. Install, update, modify, uninstall, `use`, `expose`/`hide`/`mark`/`hold`/`rollback` and a storage move are `installed`, `updated` or `removed`; collection and pin edits, seeding and unseeding are `collections-changed`; `launcher KEY` overrides and the usage facts an uninstall drops are `launchers-changed`; a start is `started`. A client that cannot hold a process open polls `vibe app launchers --revision` instead. **Arrangements across versions.** When an update replaces `org/pkg@1.0.0` by `org/pkg@1.1.0`, every collection membership, `removed` entry, pin, override and usage count keyed `org/pkg@1.0.0#id` is rewritten to `org/pkg@1.1.0#id` when the new version has a launcher `id`, keeping the user's place when seeding already appended the new key; keys whose launcher vanished are dropped. `vibe app rollback` carries them back the same way. Either is one revision bump with one `launchers-changed` event. **System projection.** `vibe app launchers --export-system [--collection NAME] [--dry-run] [--json]` writes the platform's own entries from the catalog and the user layer for the launchers with `menu = true` the user has not hidden (only the collection's, with `--collection`): on Linux `vibe-<slug>.desktop` under `$XDG_DATA_HOME/applications` (default `~/.local/share`) carrying `X-Vibe-Key` and `X-Vibe-Home`, with the icon set's PNGs copied to `icons/hicolor/<N>x<N>/apps/vibe-<slug>.png` and its SVG to `icons/hicolor/scalable/apps/vibe-<slug>.svg` (a user's own icon is named by its path instead); on Windows `<name>.lnk` under `%APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\<collection or menu_group>`, saved through Windows PowerShell's `WScript.Shell` (the tree carries no `.lnk` writer) with the icon set's `.ico` file as its icon, where it already lies in the home; on macOS `~/Applications/<name>.app`, a minimal bundle of `Info.plist` (marker key `VibeKey`), an executable `Contents/MacOS/vibe-launcher` and the icon set's `.icns` as `Resources/icon.icns`, whose executable for a `tui` or `command` launcher asks Terminal to run a `start.command` beside it. The slug is the launcher key without its version, made file-name-safe, and every entry starts `vibe app start <group>/<name>#<launcher id>` — the key without the version, so a shortcut survives an update — through the exporting `vibe`, told its home by `VIBE_SETTINGS` on Unix (a desktop session does not carry the caller's environment) or `--path` for a project home; a `gui` entry starts with `--json`, detached and recorded in the running registry, a terminal one attached. Every written path is recorded in `<home>/applications/exported.json` (`vibe-app-exported/1`: `home`, `platform`, `dry_run`, `entries` of `key`, `name`, `paths`, and `removed`), which is also the answer: a later export rewrites what it writes and removes what the record names and it no longer writes, `--dry-run` answers both lists and changes nothing, `vibe app launchers --remove-system` removes everything recorded, and an uninstall removes the entries of the package's launchers, while an update's key rewrite moves them to the new key. A removal deletes a recorded `.desktop` file only while it carries `X-Vibe-Key` and an `.app` directory only while its `Info.plist` carries `VibeKey`, so nothing vibe did not write is touched. The projection is derived and disposable: it never feeds anything back. The documents these add are `vibe-app-running/1`, `vibe-app-events/1` and `vibe-app-exported/1`; with them and the forms of `#launcher-catalog` a client needs nothing else to draw a desktop. Windows `.lnk` saving, console breaks (a `tui` launcher started under one console and stopped from another reports `terminated`, not `ended without asking`) and macOS bundles are proved by the manual tests MT-04 and MT-05, the Linux path by `cli_app_runtime`.

p.launcher-paths: Templates accept only `$app_root`, `$app_bin` (`$app_root/bin`), `$project_root` and `$vibe_home`, braced or unbraced, with `$$` for a literal dollar; expansion is one pass, never shell evaluation. A relative executable or icon resolves under `app_root`; a parent traversal, an absolute literal path, or a target outside `app_root` is refused. A working directory may resolve under `app_root` or under the selected project root; without a project, a `$project_root` point reports `requires_project` and the others stay runnable.

p.source-build: `type = "source_build"` declares zero or more `[[installation.sources]]` and one `installation.recipe`; with no sources the package tree itself is the input. Each source has a `name` (directory name), either `url` or package-relative `path`, `sha256`, and `extract` (default `true` for `.zip`, `.tar.gz`, `.tgz`; otherwise the file is kept under its own filename). The recipe has `interpreter` (as for shell) and `script`, a package-relative file. vibe fetches and verifies every source, caches downloads under the settings root at `cache/app-sources/<sha256>/`, lays them out as `<work>/sources/<name>/`, then runs the script with working directory `<work>` and environment `VIBE_SOURCES`, `VIBE_WORK`, `VIBE_OUT`, `VIBE_PACKAGE` (the package tree) and `VIBE_PLATFORM` / `VIBE_ARCH`. A zero exit with a non-empty `VIBE_OUT` directory makes `VIBE_OUT` the installed payload. `VIBE_OUT` is a staging path: the payload is moved into a library afterwards and may be moved again, so a recipe must produce a relocatable tree (relative lookup or a wrapper) and never bake the staging prefix into it; anything else fails before publication and leaves the work directory for inspection under `cache/app-build/`. `--offline` succeeds only when every source is cached.

p.storage-libraries: A library is a directory holding `vibe-library.toml` (`id`, `created`) and `apps/<slot>/<group>.<name>@<version>/` installation directories. The default library is `<settings>/opt` with id `default` and is created on first use. Additional libraries are listed in `<settings>/storage.toml` as `[[library]]` rows with `id` and absolute `path`; `vibe storage add PATH [--id ID]` creates and lists a fresh one, `attach PATH` lists an existing one whose marker id is not already configured, `detach ID` unlists without deleting, `list` shows each library with its availability and its installations. The default library cannot be detached.

p.availability: A library is available when its path is a directory whose `vibe-library.toml` carries the configured id. Availability is observed at the moment of use, never cached. An installation whose library is unavailable is listed as `unavailable` with the reason, its launchers and PATH proxies report the same reason and exit non-zero, and it is never uninstalled, moved or silently replaced as default; attaching the library again makes it ready without any further command.

p.portability: An owned installation is portable unless `[application].portable = false` or the selected option sets `portable = false`; the effective value is stored in its index record. External installations are never portable.

p.move: `vibe storage move KEY --to LIBRARY` relocates one portable owned installation: copy the directory into the destination library under a temporary name, rename it into place, rewrite the index record, then delete the source directory. A failure before the index rewrite leaves the source untouched and the destination copy an orphan; a failure after it leaves the source directory an orphan. `vibe storage gc` lists and, with `--delete`, removes directories under any available library's `apps/` that no index record references. Moving a non-portable, external or unavailable installation is refused before any copy.

p.index: `<settings>/applications/index.json` (`vibe-user-applications/3`) is the one inventory. It maps installation keys `group/name@version` to records holding the slot, package coordinate, selected option id / platform / architecture, method, `library` id and relative `directory` for owned installations or absolute `app_root` for external ones, the effective portable flag, the authored launchers and public commands, and the authored commands needed later (uninstall, force_uninstall, update, interpreter). It maps slots to their `default` installation key. The file is rewritten atomically under the existing settings lock; a failed operation never replaces a ready record. A lock another command holds is refused as `locked`, never awaited, after at most 50 ms of retrying: the lock belongs to the open file, so a child spawned while it is held shares it until the child execs, and the brief retry keeps that instant from refusing a lock already released.

p.ownership: The index is the only durable truth; `app_root` of an owned installation is derived from its library and directory at every use. Vibe deletes only directories it owns. A registered external `app_root` is used for launcher resolution and never recursively removed.

p.commands: `vibe install -g PACKAGE`, `vibe update -g PACKAGE` and `vibe uninstall -g PACKAGE` (long form `--global`) operate on one fully qualified app package in the current user's settings root, before and without any project preparation. `install -g` and `update -g` accept `--library ID` for owned methods and refuse it for external ones. A second installation of the same key replaces it in place; a different version of the same slot is added beside the existing ones. `update -g` resolves the newest matching version: an owned method installs it as a new installation and makes it the slot default when the previous default belonged to the same package; a shell method runs the authored `update` command in place. `uninstall -g` removes exactly one key: owned payload directories are deleted, external methods run the authored `uninstall`; if the removed key was the slot default, the default becomes the only remaining ready installation of that slot or `null`, and the command says which. `vibe app export` and `vibe app import FILE` carry the user home's set of applications and its launcher arrangement to another machine (`#portable-set`).

p.force-and-hooks: `pre_install` runs before the installer and `post_install` after it succeeds, both before the index is written (as steps: a leading `prepare` and a leading `finish` shell step, `PROP-065#steps`); a failing pre-hook stops before installation, a failing post-hook leaves the previous record and restores a previously placed owned payload. `--force` on install or update selects shell `force_install` or exe/msi `force_arguments`, lets an owned payload replace a directory that no index record owns, and is refused for a native method without forced arguments. `--force` on uninstall selects `force_uninstall` of an external method and is refused when none is authored; an owned installation is deleted by ordinary uninstall whatever its contents, so `--force` changes nothing for it. vibe never hashes or re-verifies an installed payload: an owned directory is trusted until it is uninstalled or replaced.

p.child-output: Installer, hook and recipe children inherit stdin and stream stdout and stderr live; in `--json` mode child stdout is relayed to stderr so the JSON envelope stays clean. The child's exit status decides success. Every installer and hook child receives `VIBE_APP_ROOT` (the installation's `app_root`); recipe children receive the variables in `#source-build`; vibe adds nothing else to the environment.

p.launcher-operations: `vibe app launchers PACKAGE --json` lists the launch points of one installation with their resolved availability. `vibe app run PACKAGE LAUNCHER [-- ARGS]` runs one point; `vibe app start PACKAGE [--launcher ID]` runs the explicit default, otherwise asks in an attended terminal and reports `selection_required` unattended. Launch resolves the template, invokes the native program with an argument array and preserves its exit status. `vibe app list` shows every installation with status and slot default.

p.alternatives: `[application].id` names a slot; every installation of that slot is a provider. Each slot has one global default. `vibe app use SLOT KEY` changes it; `vibe app alternatives SLOT` lists providers, the default and the commands each provides. Public commands of all providers in a slot are reserved for that slot; two slots may not claim the same command name. Installing the first provider of a slot makes it the default.

p.proxy: For every reserved command, `<settings>/opt/bin/<command>` (`.exe` on Windows) is a copy of the small native `vibe-app-proxy` binary. Invoked, it locates its home as the nearest ancestor of its own directory that holds `applications/index.json`, reads that index and `storage.toml`, picks the provider from `VIBE_APP_USE` (`slot=key;slot=key`) or the slot default, resolves that provider's launcher for its own command name, and executes the native program directly, forwarding arguments, exit status and, on POSIX, signals. It never runs the vibe CLI. A provider that lacks the command, an unavailable library or an absent default is a clear error with exit 127. Proxies are rewritten whenever the reserved command set changes.

p.hidden-installations: An installation may be hidden: `vibe install -g PKG --hidden` (and `vibe install PKG --hidden` in a project) performs the whole installation — payload in a library, record in the index, movable with `storage move`, updated and uninstalled like any other — but exposes nothing: no proxy in `opt/bin`, no place among the slot's alternatives, never the default. Consent, warnings and installer execution are unchanged; only exposure is withheld. `vibe app expose PKG` turns a hidden installation into an exposed one under the ordinary slot rules (an occupied slot gains an alternative, the default is not taken over); `vibe app hide PKG` is the reverse and releases the default to the next alternative when it held it. `vibe shell --with PKG[@req]` exposes a hidden installation on that session's PATH only, through `#session-selection`. `vibe app update` keeps the hidden state. `vibe app list` lists hidden installations in their own section, and `--json` carries `hidden = true`. A step requirement with build scope (PROP-065 `#app-dependencies`) is exactly a hidden installation made on a package's behalf.

p.session-selection: A session choice is the environment variable `VIBE_APP_USE`; it changes nothing in the index, the slots or `opt/bin`. Reaching an installation that has no proxy there — a hidden one through `--with`, or a build requirement on a step's PATH — needs a proxy somewhere, so vibe keeps those copies under `<home>/cache/app-proxies/<installation>/bin`, a cache like any other: rebuilt on demand, deletable at any time, never consulted by `app list` or the alternatives. `vibe shell` sets it from `--use SLOT=KEY` arguments, so two shells may run different providers of one slot concurrently while the global default stays untouched.

p.shell-command: `vibe shell [-g|--global] [--use SLOT=KEY]...` starts an interactive shell whose PATH begins with the `opt/bin` directories of the selected application homes in priority order: the project home `vibevm/vibeopt` when the working directory is a project and that home exists, then the user settings root and whose `VIBE_APP_USE` reflects the given choices. The shell executable is the caller's parent shell when it is `bash`, `zsh`, `cmd.exe`, `powershell.exe` or `pwsh.exe`, otherwise `/bin/sh` on Linux, `/bin/zsh` on macOS and the system `cmd.exe` on Windows. The command requires an attended non-JSON terminal, preserves the working directory and standard streams, and returns the shell's exit status. `-g` selects the user home alone (`#project-scope`).

p.project-scope: An application may also be installed into a project. `vibe install PACKAGE` without `-g`, run inside a project on a package of kind `app`, records the dependency in `vibe.toml` and `vibe.lock` like any other package and installs it into the project home `vibevm/vibeopt/`, which has exactly the layout of the user home: `applications/index.json`, the default library `opt/` and the proxies in `opt/bin/`; `storage.toml`, extra libraries and `vibe storage` commands apply only to the user home. `vibe install` with no arguments materialises the project's app dependencies the same way, consent-gated because installers run package-authored scripts. `vibe update`, `vibe uninstall` and `vibe app` without `-g` act on the project home when the current directory is inside a project, otherwise on the user home. `vibe shell` in `Auto` scope puts the project home's `opt/bin` before the user home's; `-g` selects the user home alone. `vibevm/vibeopt/` is ignored by git: the lockfile is the record, the directory is a materialisation. External methods installed from a project still register their system-wide `app_root` and are listed as external.

p.portable-set: The user home's applications travel as one document, protocol `vibe-apps/1` (`schemas/apps_manifest.jtd.json`), the way a Brewfile moves a toolset. `vibe app export [--output FILE] [--all] [--installations-only]` writes it as TOML on stdout or into FILE, and `--json` prints the same document as JSON; `-g` is implied, and only an explicit `--path` exports a project home, which the document says as `home = "project"`. The head names the protocol, the RFC 3339 `exported` time, `home`, and the exporting host's `platform` and `arch`, which are informative. One `[[application]]` per installation carries its exact `key`, the `installer` option id chosen on the exporting host, `features`, `parameters` (never a secret one, as the index keeps them), `license = "accepted"` only when a licence was accepted, `mark` (`manual` or `auto`), and `held = true` / `hidden = true` when so; hidden installations and `auto` rows are written only with `--all`, and a kept previous version never. Unless `--installations-only`, the user's launcher arrangement follows with the words of `launchers.toml` (`#launcher-catalog`): `[[collection]]` with `name` and `launchers`, `[[pin]]` with `target` (`taskbar` or `favorites`, as `vibe app pin` names them) and its ordered `launchers`, and `[[launcher]]` overrides with `key` and only the fields the user changed (`name`, `hidden`, `icon`). `vibe app import FILE [--dry-run] [--registry DIR] [--accept-license] [--skip-installed]` reads TOML or JSON into the user home and refuses `--path`, because a project records its applications in `vibe.toml`. Each `manual` row resolves its exact version through the ordinary path, `--registry` first and the configured registries for what it does not carry, and installs through the ordinary `install -g` operation with its plan, panel, licence question and requirements, one row after another: the row's `installer` when this host's detected platform and architecture offer an option of that id, otherwise the option the host is detected to take (the rule `--platform`, `--arch` and `--installer` left out apply); the row's features are chosen and the defaults it left out deselected, and features and parameters the chosen option does not declare are dropped. `auto` rows install only as requirements of a manual row. A licence is asked as `install -g` asks it unless `--accept-license`; under `--unattended` an unaccepted licence refuses that row with `license_required`. A key already installed with the same option, features and parameters is skipped; with another choice it is refused with `choice_differs`, naming `vibe app modify`, and `--skip-installed` makes it a skip instead. A `held` row is held after it installs. A row whose package cannot be resolved, or whose installation fails, is a refusal of that row only, with the error's own code; the others go on. The arrangement is merged after the installations under the home's mutation lock: a collection is created or extended by name, a pinned list gains the keys it lacks in the document's order, an override sets the fields it carries, and a key naming no launcher of the home (its package was refused or skipped) is skipped with the reason. `--dry-run` resolves and decides every row, prints one row per application as `install`, `skip` or `refuse` with its reason, and changes nothing. The trailer counts installed, skipped and refused rows; `--json` answers `vibe-app-import/1` (`schemas/application_import.jtd.json`) with `home`, `dry_run`, `installed`, `skipped` (`key`, `reason`) and `refused` (`key`, `code`, `message`), and `licenses` (`key`, `name`, `file`, emitted when empty) names, in a dry run and a real run alike, each installing row whose chosen option declares a licence this home has not accepted for that key and that `--accept-license` does not cover through the row's `license = "accepted"`, with `file` the absolute path of the text in the resolved package as `vibe app describe` reports it, so a caller shows the text before the run; the human dry run lists those as `license KEY NAME` rows. The command exits 1 when any row was refused. An unreadable document refuses the whole import with `apps_file_invalid`.

p.acceptance: The gate for every method and command is one public CLI fixture under an isolated settings root: install → list → launch through `app run` and through the PATH proxy → alternatives switch → uninstall. Source_build is proven with a package-local script and two sources (one URL served locally, one package-local file). Storage is proven with two libraries: install into the second, detach, observe `unavailable`, attach, move to the default, `gc` after a simulated interruption. Shell is proven on Linux in a pseudo-terminal. Windows and macOS behaviour is proven on the owner's native machines with the manual tests under `vibevm/vibespecs/manual-tests/`, not by cross-compilation.

p.decisions: Decision: plain files and atomic rename instead of transactional journals. Why: the October prototype grew to 350k lines and an uninstall read 187 GB while chasing crash-proof publication; the owner's requirement was "report a missing disk", not survive it transactionally. Rejected: journals with recovery (unbounded proof cost), a separate build lifecycle for recipes (couples applications to the project build planes). Revisit when a real user loses installation state to an interruption that `storage gc` cannot explain.
